passages.t: ‘They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Maskil of Asaph” (verse 1). Maskil is a word for a kind of psalm whose meaning is uncertain. Then the first cry: “Why have You rejected us forever, O God? Why does Your anger smolder against the sheep of Your pasture?” (verse 1).

The people ask God to come and look at the ruins (verse 3). Then they describe what the enemy did, scene by scene, as if walking God through it. Soldiers shouted in the holy place and set up their banners (verse 4). They hacked at the carved wood like men chopping a thicket (verses 5 to 6). “They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground; they have defiled the dwelling place of Your Name” (verse 7).

Worst of all, God seems silent. “There are no signs for us to see. There is no longer any prophet. And none of us knows how long this will last” (verse 9). So they ask, “How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You?” (verse 10). And they beg him to stop holding back his hand (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is a psalm for the worst day in Israel's history before the time of Jesus. Most scholars connect it with the year 587 or 586 BC, when the army of Babylon burned Jerusalem and its temple, as the book page says. The Bible tells it plainly: “He burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem” (2 Kings 25:9). Some have suggested a later attack on the temple, but a sanctuary ‘burned to the ground’ fits Babylon best. Since Asaph lived in David's day, the psalm must come from a later singer of his line.

To a hearer in the ancient world, a burned temple meant more than a burned building. People believed a temple was the house of a god. When a city's temple fell, the nations around said its god had lost. That is why the enemy's banners in the holy place (verse 4) hurt so much. They were a claim of victory over the LORD himself.

Notice the grief and the anger. The people do not hide either one. They bring both to God. They even tell him what to do: ‘Stretch it out to destroy them’ (verse 11). The book page's part on the cursing psalms explains how Christians read prayers like that.
passages.later:
The book of Lamentations mourns the same ruin: “The Lord has rejected His altar; He has abandoned His sanctuary” (Lamentations 2:7). Lamentations and Psalm 74 are two voices of one grief.

Centuries later a second temple stood on the same hill. Jesus said of it, “not one stone here will be left on another” (Matthew 24:2). He also said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again” (John 2:19), and John explains that he meant his own body.
passages.asks:
Have you ever stood in a ruin, a marriage, a church, a home, a hope, and asked God how long? Psalm 74 gives you permission to describe the damage to God in detail, as these singers did. You do not have to tidy your grief before you pray it.

Notice also what they ask God to remember: the people he bought and the place he chose (verse 2). In the ruins, they remind God of his own promises.

passages.t: ‘Yet God is my King from ancient times’
passages.happening:
In the middle of the ruins the psalm turns to remembering. “Yet God is my King from ancient times, working salvation on the earth” (verse 12).

Then come pictures of God's power. “You divided the sea by Your strength; You smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea” (verse 13). “You crushed the heads of Leviathan” (verse 14). God made springs flow and rivers dry up (verse 15). He made day and night, sun and moon, the borders of the earth, summer and winter (verses 16 to 17).

Then the psalm turns back to asking. “Do not deliver the soul of Your dove to beasts” (verse 19). Israel is the dove, small and helpless. “Consider Your covenant” (verse 20). “Rise up, O God; defend Your cause” (verse 22).

The psalm ends with no answer yet. Its last line is the noise of God's enemies, still rising (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Leviathan was a monster of the sea in the old stories of Israel's neighbours. In texts found at Ugarit, an ancient city on the coast of Syria, the god Baal defeats a sea monster with seven heads. Scholars connect that monster, often called Litan or Lotan, with the Leviathan of the Bible. In those stories the sea stood for chaos, the wild power that threatens life.

Psalm 74 takes that picture and gives the victory to the LORD, not to Baal. It is a bold claim. The enemy thinks Israel's God has lost. The psalm answers that he is the King who tamed the sea itself. Some readers also hear the Red Sea here, when God ‘divided the sea’ for Israel to cross (Exodus 14:21). Others hear the making of the world. The poem may mean both.

This was a daring thing to sing in a burned city. Nothing they could see said God was King. They sang it anyway.
passages.later:
Isaiah uses the same picture of the end of days: “He will slay the dragon of the sea” (Isaiah 27:1). He also prays, “Was it not You who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep” (Isaiah 51:10).

In Revelation, John sees the last victory over chaos: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more” (Revelation 21:1).
passages.asks:
When nothing you see says that God is in charge, what do you remember? This psalm reached back to the oldest things it knew about God, and held them up beside the ruins.

The psalm also ends without being answered. That is allowed. You may stop praying for the day with your question still open, and come back to it tomorrow.
